title: Signature-Informed Transformer for Asset Allocation
one_liner: The paper trains one portfolio policy end to end, using path summaries of price history and a risk-based objective so the learned allocation is judged by bad-loss control rather than forecast error alone.
lead: Portfolio systems often split the job into two separate stages. First they predict future returns. Then they hand those predictions to an optimizer that chooses portfolio weights. That split is convenient, but it can point learning at the wrong target because a small forecasting mistake can matter a lot for the final allocation while a larger mistake may matter little. This paper combines representation learning and portfolio choice into one policy. It summarizes each asset path with a compact ordered-history description, compares assets through a learned cross-asset weighting step, and trains the whole system directly against downside risk.

problem.h2: Why return prediction alone is not enough for allocation
paras: An allocation rule has to decide how much capital to place in each asset. A standard pipeline predicts future returns for each asset and then solves a separate optimization step. The trouble is that the training signal in the first stage rewards accurate forecasts, not good portfolio decisions. A model can reduce average forecast error and still build a weak portfolio because the forecast misses the patterns that matter most for joint risk.

The paper starts from the view that allocation should be trained on the quantity the investor actually cares about: the shape of losses after assets interact inside one portfolio. That requires one model that reads path history, compares assets, and outputs weights under a risk objective.

callout.html: Forecasting and allocation are usually trained apart, so the system learns to predict prices rather than to choose weights that control bad portfolio outcomes.

panels.title: 1. Two-stage pipeline
panels.viz_args: price history -> return forecast -> separate optimizer
panels.caption: The forecast stage is judged on prediction error, even though the final goal is portfolio risk.

panels.title: 2. What gets lost
panels.caption: Important path structure can be blurred when the model compresses everything into one next-return guess.

panels.title: 3. Summarize each path
panels.viz_args: ordered price moves -> compact path summary
panels.caption: The model keeps track of ordered moves so it can use more than one-step prediction cues.

panels.title: 4. Compare assets jointly
panels.caption: The policy decides weights after looking across assets together, because allocation depends on relative roles inside the whole basket.

panels.title: 5. Train on downside risk
panels.caption: The system is trained to reduce the worst losses directly, so the learning target matches the portfolio objective.

steps.text: Turn the recent ordered price path of each asset into a compact path summary because the order of gains and losses can matter for allocation even when one-step summary statistics look similar.

steps.b: Project assets into one shared space.
steps.text: Map all asset summaries into a common comparison space so the policy can judge which assets play similar or different roles inside the portfolio.
Use a learned weighting step across assets so each asset weight depends on the others, because allocation is a joint decision rather than a set of isolated bets.
Convert the joint comparison result into capital weights across assets for the next rebalance period.
Adjust the whole policy to reduce conditional value at risk, because that objective punishes severe losses in the worst set of return outcomes.

paras: The paper changes the training target and the internal representation at the same time. It replaces a forecast-first pipeline with one learned policy that reads asset paths and is optimized directly for portfolio downside risk.
object.object: the mapping from market history to portfolio weights

hidden.name: how much each asset path contributes to future portfolio tail risk
paras: The hidden quantity is not the next return of one asset by itself. It is the contribution that each asset path makes to the bad-loss region of the whole portfolio. Two assets with similar expected returns can deserve very different weights because one tends to amplify losses when the rest of the portfolio is already under stress.

The path summary and cross-asset weighting step help estimate that quantity because they preserve ordered movement patterns and compare assets jointly. Direct risk training then keeps the model focused on the set of outcomes that matters most for allocation.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark signals that help the policy judge which paths worsen or soften the portfolio's worst outcomes.

reads.html: The system is trying to detect which assets will make the portfolio's bad days even worse and which assets will cushion them, because that is what weight choice really needs.
The learned policy estimates tail-relevant cross-asset structure from path summaries and uses that estimate to set weights under a conditional-value-at-risk objective.

mechanism.h2: Why the combined policy can beat a forecast-first pipeline
paras: The model helps when useful allocation information is path dependent and cross-asset because a forecast-only pipeline usually compresses history into one return estimate per asset. That loses information when the order of moves matters, such as steady decline followed by rebound versus quiet drift followed by a sharp drop. The path summary keeps some of that ordered structure.

The joint weighting step matters because portfolio choice is relative. An asset should receive a larger or smaller weight depending on what the other assets are doing at the same time. Training the full system on downside risk closes the objective gap because the model is rewarded for changing weights in ways that reduce bad-tail outcomes, not for chasing lower prediction error that may not improve the portfolio.

stages.s: recent price paths for all assets

math.h2: Train the policy on conditional value at risk
math.words: Choose policy settings that make the average loss in the worst alpha fraction of portfolio outcomes as small as possible.
symbols: the portfolio return produced by the policy over one holding period
the loss threshold that marks the worst alpha fraction of outcomes
the average loss inside that worst alpha fraction
the chosen tail fraction, such as the worst 5 percent of outcomes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose five portfolio outcomes are 3, 1, -2, -4, and -9 percent.
Take alpha = 0.2, so we focus on the worst 20 percent of outcomes.
The worst 20 percent here is the single outcome -9 percent.
Its average loss is 9 percent, so conditional value at risk is 9 percent.
A new policy with worst outcome -6 percent would have lower conditional value at risk, so it is preferred because its bad tail is less severe.

math.note: The paper optimizes this tail-loss target directly, which keeps learning aligned with allocation quality rather than forecast error alone.

charts.title: Forecast-first baselines
charts.note: These systems leave money-management structure unused because their training target is still prediction accuracy rather than direct downside control.

charts.title: Signature-Informed policy
charts.note: The paper reports stronger portfolio results because the learned path summaries and joint weighting step are trained against the same risk criterion used at decision time.

items.b: Path summaries can overfit one market regime.
items.html: If the training period contains a narrow style of price behavior, the learned policy can rely on path patterns that stop mattering later because the market regime changes.

items.b: Tail-risk training can become unstable with little data.
items.html: Conditional value at risk uses rare bad outcomes, so the target can be noisy when the sample of stressed periods is small because a few extreme episodes dominate learning.

items.b: Joint weighting can amplify noisy cross-asset relations.
items.html: If many assets move together for accidental reasons in the training set, the policy can assign exaggerated roles to those relations because it treats them as persistent structure.

The method works when path summaries capture recurring market structure and enough stressed periods are available, because then direct tail-risk training can separate useful diversifiers from loss amplifiers.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small daily-rebalanced portfolio simulator on a handful of assets. Compare two systems on the same rolling windows. The first predicts next-period returns and then applies a standard optimizer. The second reads recent paths, outputs weights directly, and is trained on conditional value at risk. Include one market period where path order matters, such as calm drift followed by clustered losses.

The demo should show that the direct policy gives better bad-tail control because it can change weights based on ordered path patterns and cross-asset roles instead of relying only on one-step return accuracy.
demo.closing: The decisive result is lower bad-tail loss at similar or better average return, because that shows the model learned allocation-relevant structure rather than only forecast accuracy.
